strengths: Pioneering direction: the paper positions itself as the first multimodal time series foundation model supporting both text/image inputs and zero-shot cross-domain inference, a clear gap between unimodal TSFMs (Sundial, MOIRAI, Chronos) and end-to-end multimodal supervised models (GPT4MTS, CALF, Time-VLM).

Comprehensive and well-organized empirical evaluation on three recognized benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS) with 10 foundation-model baselines and 8 supervised baselines, plus full per-horizon results in the appendix; large margins are reported on most datasets (e.g., 27.0% MSE reduction vs. Sundial on TimeMMD zero-shot).

The proposed components are technically coherent: modality-guided attention injection via a bridged correlation matrix (Eq. 12-16), token distillation with learnable semantic centroid queries, and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching that replaces the Gaussian starting point of flow matching with retrieved period/trend prototypes, which is a sensible and well-motivated use of the stochastic-interpolant property of flow matching.

Ablation studies (Table 4) cover all major modules and show consistent degradation, and the paper addresses known evaluation pitfalls (drop_last=False, exclusion of pretraining datasets, context-length selection per baseline paper).

Efficiency analysis (Table 8) and inference-scalability analysis (Figure 5) are included, and pretraining details (corpus composition, patch/token configuration, compute budget) are reported in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Potential information leakage in the pretraining text modality: the GPT4-generated sample-wise descriptions (Figure 7) explicitly describe the future trend of the corresponding segment ('analyze the future trend ... significant decline and a continuous downward trend'). If the text can implicitly encode future values, the model may learn to extract forecasts from text rather than genuine domain knowledge, inflating multimodal gains. The paper does not discuss or control for this risk, and does not ablate with future-agnostic text.

Incremental novelty at the component level: token distillation via learnable cross-attention queries is established (e.g., Perceiver/Bottleneck-style, Crossformer), adding a bias term to attention scores is a simple mechanism, and prototype-guided flow matching is a relatively small modification of standard conditional OT flow matching. The contribution is more of an engineering combination than a conceptual advance, and no theoretical analysis of why prototype initialization improves flow matching is provided.

The image modality is endogenously derived from the same series (FFT-period-based rendering, following VisionTS), so its claimed added value over the time modality is questionable; no ablation isolates the image branch's contribution separately from text.

Some evaluation asymmetries remain: multimodal zero-shot comparisons are only against unimodal foundation models, and the strong claims rest largely on few-shot (10%) vs. full-shot comparisons where Aurora still uses pretrained knowledge; statistical significance tests and variance over seeds are not reported.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue: numerous typos throughout ('Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'hevay', 'pionnering', 'merticulously', 'Inituitively', 'propriate', 'inital', 'Scability'), duplicated references (Dai et al. 2024a/b/c), and some imprecise claims (e.g., 'correlation matrix contains domain knowledge') that reduce clarity.

Aurora is the most expensive model at inference (83.5 ms, 18.3G MACs, 418.6M parameters in Table 8) while many reported gains are modest on some datasets (e.g., Security and parts of TSFM-Bench), and the cost-accuracy trade-off is not analyzed.

strengths: Addresses a timely and meaningful problem: combining cross-modal domain knowledge (text, endogenous images) with time series foundation models to enable zero-shot cross-domain forecasting; the positioning of multimodal TSFMs vs. unimodal TSFMs and end-to-end supervised multimodal models is well motivated.

Broad empirical coverage: evaluation spans three recognized benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS) with 10 foundation model baselines and 8 end-to-end supervised models, and the paper addresses the drop_last evaluation pitfall, which shows awareness of recent benchmarking concerns.

Includes ablation studies of the two main novel components (Modality-Guided Attention and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching) and an efficiency analysis, and the pretraining corpus construction (1B+ points across 8 domains) represents substantial engineering effort.
weaknesses: Poor writing quality throughout the manuscript: pervasive typos and grammatical errors (e.g., 'Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'hevay', 'capabilites', 'pionnering', 'inituitively', 'propriate', 'merticulously', 'Scability', 'supversied', 'tutor' for 'teach', 'GTP4MTS' variants) that should have been caught before submission and undermine confidence in overall care.

Serious citation integrity concerns: the reference list contains clearly irrelevant, padded citations (e.g., Lu et al. on diffusion watermarking and concept erasure, soccer commentary generation, text-motion generation, video understanding agents) that have no connection to time series forecasting; Dai et al. 2024a/b/c is the same paper listed three times; ERA5 is cited as (Liu et al., 2025d), which is the Sundial paper. This pattern of citation padding is a red flag.

Novelty is incremental: the components are largely assembled from existing techniques — BERT/ViT encoders, learnable-query token distillation (Perceiver-style), attention-bias injection resembling Crossformer, and flow matching with a modified (prototype-based) prior. Prototype-guided initialization of flow matching is a modest modification, and the claim of 'pioneering' multimodal TSFMs is overstated given prior paired-text work (e.g., TATS, ChatTS-style approaches).

The 'multimodal domain knowledge' is synthetic: pretraining texts are generated by GPT-4 from the raw series themselves, so the model may simply be learning to exploit LLM-paraphrased descriptions of historical statistics rather than genuine external domain knowledge. This raises questions about generalization to real-world text and about whether the huge zero-shot gains (e.g., Economy MSE 0.033 vs. 0.29 for all baselines, a ~10x gap that is not analyzed or explained) reflect a distribution artifact.

The headline results are driven by comparisons that are not apples-to-apples: on TimeMMD zero-shot, unimodal foundation models (Sundial, VisionTS, ROSE, etc.) are denied access to text, so the large margins primarily measure the extra modality rather than the proposed architecture. On the fair unimodal comparisons (TSFM-Bench, ProbTS), the gains over the strongest baselines are small (e.g., ETT avg 0.331 vs. 0.335 for Sundial), and Sundial is better on Electricity; the claimed '15.1% MSE reduction vs Time-MoE' relies on a weaker baseline.

Incomplete analysis and weak evidential support: no variance/std or statistical significance across runs; ablations are only conducted on TimeMMD and not on the unimodal benchmarks; no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (prototype bank size M, number of distilled tokens K, steps J); the Security dataset results (MSE ~72 for all models) suggest a problematic setup that is not discussed.

Comparison protocol against full-shot supervised models mixes zero-shot and few-shot (10%) settings without a clear justification or a full fine-tuning comparison of the proposed model, making it hard to assess whether the multimodal pretraining itself (vs. simply more data/modality) drives the improvements.

strengths: Aurora is positioned as one of the first multimodal time series foundation models, combining text/image endogenous modalities with zero-shot cross-domain inference—this addresses a real gap between unimodal TSFMs (no explicit domain knowledge) and end-to-end multimodal models (no zero-shot capability), and the motivation (similar histories, different futures across domains) is clearly articulated.

The technical design is thoughtful: token distillation via learnable query vectors for compression, the Modality-Guided Multi-head Self-Attention that injects cross-modal correlation (Corr) into temporal attention is a concrete and interesting mechanism, and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching—initializing the ODE from retrieved periodic/trend prototypes rather than Gaussian noise—is a sensible use of flow matching's stochastic-interpolant flexibility.

Evaluation is extensive and broad: 10 unimodal foundation models and 8 end-to-end supervised baselines across three recognized benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS), covering zero-shot, few-shot, deterministic and probabilistic settings, with full per-horizon results in the appendix, ablations of both core modules, inference scalability analysis, and an efficiency comparison.

The paper handles known pitfalls in time series evaluation (e.g., the 'drop_last' issue) and states the benchmark datasets are strictly excluded from pretraining, which supports fair zero-shot claims.
The modality-absence scenario (random text masking during pretraining) is a practical consideration and strengthens the generality claims.
weaknesses: The 'multimodal' corpus relies on LLM-generated (GPT-4) textual descriptions of raw time series, which are essentially simulated restatements of the series themselves. This weakens the claim that Aurora learns genuine external domain knowledge during pretraining—it may largely be learning to exploit information already present in the history window, and the downstream text distributions (e.g., TimeMMD) may not match the GPT-4 generated pretraining text distribution. The paper does not analyze text quality or distribution shift.

Writing quality is below the standard for a top-tier venue: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'hevay', 'merticulously', 'pionnering', 'Scability', 'inital', 'propriate'), which suggests insufficient polish and slightly undermines confidence in overall rigor.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence. 'Pioneering the exploration of multimodal time series foundation model' is asserted, but related work (e.g., language-paired time series like Li et al. 2025d, Chatts, TimeMMD-based models) should be more carefully differentiated. The abstract/introduction also frame cross-domain gains as coming from 'domain knowledge,' yet the ablation cannot isolate whether gains come from text content vs. simply more parameters/supervision from an auxiliary modality.

Prototype-Guided Flow Matching is a relatively incremental modification of standard conditional flow matching (OT path, MLP + AdaLN are borrowed from DiT/Flow Matching); the contribution is the prototype initialization, whose benefit is not analyzed beyond end-to-end ablations (e.g., no comparison to simply conditioning on prototypes, or analysis of prototype quality/retrieval behavior).

The few-shot comparison is somewhat confounded: Aurora is a foundation model pretrained on a large cross-domain corpus and then fine-tuned on 10% of downstream data, compared against full-shot end-to-end models trained on 100%—this is a legitimate setting but the paper's framing ('outperforms all baselines in most settings') could mislead about the source of the advantage.

Several baselines have missing entries ('-') due to pretraining overlap or excessive compute, and table footnotes about dataset exclusions are only visible in the appendix; on datasets like Security (MSE ~70) the averages are dominated by scale effects. Statistical significance tests or variance across seeds are not reported.

Pretraining scale (~1B points, 8 GPUs, 30 days) is modest relative to the foundation-model framing and scaling-law arguments cited; no scaling analysis is provided to support the generality of the approach.

The related-work appendix (Section C) reads as citation padding with loosely related references, and the Corr = VAttn·W·TAttn^T construction in Eq. (14) bridges time-time correlations via a rank-K^image × K^text bilinear map whose inductive bias is not well justified theoretically.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored direction: a multimodal time series foundation model that supports both text/image inputs and zero-shot cross-domain inference, distinguishing itself from unimodal foundation models and end-to-end multimodal supervised models.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 recognized benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS, TFB, EPF) with a large and relevant baseline set (11 foundation models plus supervised/multimodal baselines), covering deterministic, probabilistic, zero-shot, few-shot, and short-term settings.

Several concrete technical components are clearly described: Modality-Guided Multi-head Self-Attention with a bridged Corr matrix, token distillation via learnable query vectors, and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching that initializes the interpolant from retrieved prototypes rather than standard Gaussian noise.

Reasonable ablation studies (removing modality guidance, prototype mechanism, and individual modalities), prototype bank size analysis, inference scalability analysis with sampled predictions, attention-weight visualizations, and an efficiency comparison; the 'drop_last' evaluation detail is handled transparently.

Reproducibility statement with released code/checkpoints, detailed appendix including pretraining corpus composition, baseline repositories, dataset statistics, metrics definitions, and model configuration.
weaknesses: A central methodological concern: the pretraining corpus text is synthetically generated by GPT4 from the raw series, and the prompts (Figure 8) explicitly ask GPT4 to 'analyze the future trend' of the sample. If generated descriptions contain information derived from the sample's future behavior, the multimodal pretraining signal may partly constitute label leakage, inflating apparent gains from the text modality. The paper does not quantify how much of the multimodal benefit stems from real transferable domain knowledge versus such leakage.

The paper's claim of being the 'first multimodal time series foundation model' is overstated given prior work on multimodal time series models (GPT4MTS, TATS, Time-VLM, TimeMMD ecosystem, ChatTS, etc.); novelty of the architectural components (cross-attention distillers/guiders, flow matching with a modified start distribution) is incremental rather than fundamental.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue: numerous typos and inconsistencies throughout ('Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'merticulously', 'hevay', 'pionnering', 'GTP4MTS', 'scability', 'Supversied'), a missing ROSE repository entry and other reference/repository errors, which undermines polish and reproducibility.

Aurora has notably high compute cost (18.329 G MACs and 83.5 ms inference, the worst or near-worst in Table 9) and requires 8x A800 GPUs for 30 days; the practicality/efficiency trade-off is acknowledged only briefly and no efficiency-oriented ablation is provided.

Ablation studies are conducted only on TimeMMD (multimodal) settings; there are no ablations on unimodal benchmarks (TSFM-Bench/ProbTS), and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals for any of the comparisons.

Some benchmark results are mixed (e.g., EPF Table 4 where Aurora loses to full-shot supervised models on several markets, and Security where Sundial's zero-shot results are competitive), but the text overstates the consistency of SOTA performance; '1st Count' tallies also mask that many datasets in Table 13/14 have missing baselines ('-'), which complicates fair comparison.

Tension in the evaluation design: comparing zero-shot Aurora against full-shot supervised models, and excluding some datasets from some baselines' evaluation, makes the headline percentage improvements difficult to interpret without careful reading.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful gap: a time series foundation model that can consume multimodal (text/image) inputs while still supporting zero-shot inference, which neither unimodal TSFMs nor end-to-end multimodal supervised models currently do.

Evaluation is broad in scope: five benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS, TFB, EPF) covering unimodal, multimodal, deterministic, and probabilistic settings, with a large number of baselines (11 foundation models plus supervised models), per-horizon full results in the appendix, ablations on the main components and modalities, efficiency analysis, and qualitative visualizations including attention-weight case studies.

The framing of 'similar histories leading to different futures across domains' is an interesting motivating observation, and the prototype visualization (Appendix C) and modality-guided attention analyses give some interpretability.
weaknesses: Serious risk of information leakage in the pretraining corpus. The GPT4-generated textual descriptions (Figure 8) are explicitly asked to 'analyze the future trend and characteristics' of the series, and the generated texts contain statements like 'the future trend might show a slow upward recovery' or 'the electricity consumption is expected to continue to decrease.' If such texts are paired with the very horizons the model must predict, the text modality may leak future information during pretraining, undermining the core claim of cross-domain generalization. The paper never analyzes whether descriptions reference the evaluation window, nor does it ablate with future-free descriptions. The enormous gains on some datasets (e.g., Economy: 0.033 vs. 0.291 for the next best model, ~9x improvement) raise the suspicion of such leakage and are not convincingly explained.

Limited technical novelty. Each component is a recombination of existing techniques: token distillation is standard Perceiver-style learnable-query cross-attention; the modality-guided attention (Eq. 14-16) is essentially adding a learned bias to attention logits, and the claim that Corr = VAttn·W·TAttn^T meaningfully 'bridges' temporal correlations through a text-image cross product is asserted rather than justified; starting flow matching from a non-Gaussian prior is already explored (e.g., Kollovieh et al., which the paper cites). The endogenous-image pathway closely follows VisionTS. The 'first multimodal time series foundation model' claim is overstated given TimeMMD/TATS/Time-VLM-style multimodal work.

Unfair or mismatched comparisons in places. The headline multimodal zero-shot comparison pits Aurora (with privileged text and image inputs) against unimodal foundation models; percentage-improvement figures in Figure 4 are computed over selective subsets while some datasets (e.g., Security, parts of EPF) show Aurora losing. Averaging and '1st count' summaries obscure this, and the claimed 15.1%/22.9% improvements vs. Time-MoE/ROSE are hard to verify given many '-' entries in Table 13.

Reproducibility statement is literally broken: 'We have released our model code and checkpoints on and .' with empty link placeholders. Combined with pervasive typos and grammatical errors ('Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'hevay', 'capabilites', 'merticulously', 'Supversied'), a missing ROSE repository in Table 6, and duplicated references (Dai et al. 2024a/b), the manuscript gives the impression of insufficient care.

The reference list contains numerous clearly irrelevant citations (image watermarking, diffusion concept erasure, soccer commentary generation, video understanding agents), which appear to be citation stuffing and undermine trust in the related-work discussion.

Aurora is the most computationally expensive model evaluated (18.329 G MACs, 83.5 ms inference — the worst in Table 9), yet the paper downplays this as 'moderate efficiency.' For a foundation model claiming practical out-of-the-box utility, this cost, plus the 30-day pretraining on 8x A800, is a significant practical limitation.

No statistical significance, variance across seeds, or uncertainty on the reported averages; given that many margins in Tables 2-3 are small (e.g., vs. Sundial on ETTm1/Weather), the 'state-of-the-art' claim is fragile.

The claimed motivation (domain knowledge resolving similar histories) is only loosely connected to the evaluation: most benchmarks are standard unimodal/multimodal forecasting where 'similar history, different future' is not directly tested; the showcased examples in Appendix C are anecdotal.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: a multimodal time series foundation model that supports both zero-shot inference and text/image modality injection, bridging two previously separate lines of research (unimodal TSFMs and end-to-end multimodal supervised models). This 'first' positioning is plausible and clearly motivated.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive: five benchmarks (TimeMMD, TSFM-Bench, ProbTS, TFB with 8,068 univariate series, EPF), covering zero-shot, few-shot, deterministic, and probabilistic settings, with a large and modern baseline set including 11 foundation models and multiple multimodal end-to-end models.

The technical design is coherent: token distillation via learnable queries, a Modality-Guided Multi-head Self-Attention that injects cross-modal correlation matrices into temporal attention, and Prototype-Guided Flow Matching that starts the ODE from retrieved prototypes rather than Gaussian noise.

Good analytical depth: component ablations (Tables 5, 18, 19), prototype-bank size study (Table 17), inference scalability study (Figure 6), efficiency analysis (Table 9, Figure 9), attention-weight visualizations (Figures 18-21), and the 'drop_last' fairness treatment shows awareness of known benchmarking pitfalls.

Handles modality absence gracefully (random masking during pretraining), so the model remains competitive as a unimodal zero-shot forecaster, making the contribution more robust than text-only multimodal designs.
Appropriate treatment of data hygiene: claims that benchmark datasets are strictly excluded from the pretraining corpus, and shared datasets across benchmarks are reported with exclusions.
weaknesses: Potentially serious validity concern with the pretraining corpus: the textual descriptions are generated by GPT-4 from raw series, and the prompts (Figure 8) explicitly ask the LLM to 'analyze the future trend' of the time series. The generated text therefore appears to encode future information, and pretraining on such text risks teaching a shortcut (forecasting from textual trend descriptions) rather than genuine cross-domain knowledge transfer. The paper does not analyze or ablate this risk, and it is unclear how much of the multimodal gain transfers to settings with real exogenous text.

The 'image modality' is a deterministic transformation of the same time series (FFT-based period folding, rendering, repeat channels). It adds no exogenous information, yet Table 18 shows Time-Only is dramatically worse than Time+Image. This suggests the gains may come from architectural/auxiliary-effects rather than image 'geometric information', and the paper does not explain this discrepancy or control for it (e.g., comparing to a model with equal extra capacity/patches).

Novelty of individual components is incremental: token distillation via learnable queries is borrowed from perceiver-style designs, the Corr-injected attention is a modification of standard attention, and non-Gaussian initial distributions for flow matching have been explored (e.g., Kollovieh et al.'s GP-prior flow matching, which is cited). The paper's contribution is more a well-executed system than a fundamentally new technique.

Reproducibility statement claims code and checkpoints are released, but the URLs are literally blank ('released ... on and .'), and the ROSE baseline's repository is missing in Table 6. Given no verifiable code link, reproducibility cannot be confirmed.

Corpus overlap is asserted rather than demonstrated: several pretraining sources come from TFB and Monash (FRED_MD, NN5, Sunspot, Temperature Rain, etc.), while one evaluation benchmark is TFB's 8,068 univariate datasets. The paper only says the datasets are 'from different sources'; a formal de-duplication check (e.g., by series identity/statistics) is not provided.

Writing quality is below bar for a top venue: numerous typos and grammatical errors throughout ('Corss-domain', 'corrsponding', 'hevay', 'Tranformer', 'pionnering', 'merticulously', 'capabilites', 'inituitively', 'Retreiver', 'propriate'), which distracts and suggests insufficient polish.

No statistical significance reporting (std over seeds) for any headline results, despite generative sampling introducing stochasticity; gains on some benchmarks (e.g., EPF, TFB) are small and could be within noise.

Efficiency is a weakness acknowledged but under-discussed: Aurora has the highest MACs (18.3G) and slowest inference (83.5ms) among compared foundation models, which conflicts somewhat with the 'out-of-the-box decision intelligence tool' framing.

Some baselines are excluded on many datasets ('-' marks), and in Table 3 several supervised models are marked '/' for 'excessive time consumption'; the resulting head-to-head coverage is uneven across datasets.
